lead: A hole, a groove or a sharp shoulder makes the lines of stress crowd together, and the local stress can be two or three times the stress the simple formulas give. The theoretical stress concentration factor K<sub>t</sub> measures this rise for the geometry alone. Under repeated load a real material feels only part of it: the notch sensitivity q turns K<sub>t</sub> into the fatigue notch factor K<sub>f</sub>. Shaft shoulders, keyways, oil holes, bolt threads and crane hooks all need this correction, and a few millimetres of fillet radius can decide whether a part survives a million cycles.
prereq: You need: the bending and torsion stress formulas (see Direct, bending and torsional stresses) and the chapter on theories of failure for comparing a local stress with a strength.

blocks.text: Far from a notch the stress follows the simple formula; at the notch root it rises to a sharp peak. The theoretical (geometric) stress concentration factor is the ratio of the two:

σ<sub>max</sub> is the highest local elastic stress at the notch and σ<sub>nom</sub> is the nominal stress on the net section at the notch for the same load, both in MPa. K<sub>t</sub> is a pure number and depends only on the shape and the type of load, not on the material.

Take σ<sub>nom</sub> on the net section, because the charts were drawn that way. For a stepped shaft in bending σ<sub>nom</sub> = 32M/(πd³) with d the smaller diameter; in torsion σ<sub>nom</sub> = 16T/(πd³); for an axial load on a plate with a hole σ<sub>nom</sub> = P/A<sub>net</sub> with A<sub>net</sub> = (w − d)t, where w is the width, d the hole diameter and t the thickness.

An elliptical hole in a wide plate has K<sub>t</sub> = 1 + 2a/b (a the half-axis across the load, b along it): a circle gives 3 and a thin slit a very large value, which is why cracks grow. A central hole in a plate of width w has K<sub>t</sub> = 2 + (1 − d/w)³ on the net section (Heywood). For fillets, keyways and grooves read K<sub>t</sub> from Peterson-type charts using D/d and r/d, or find it by photoelasticity or finite elements.

sections.h3: Notch sensitivity and the fatigue notch factor

blocks.text: Under repeated load the fatigue strength of a notched bar falls by a factor K<sub>f</sub> that is usually smaller than K<sub>t</sub>, because the steep stress gradient at a small notch leaves the material around it to help. The notch sensitivity q says what fraction of the theoretical rise is felt:
q runs from 0 (the material ignores the notch, K<sub>f</sub> = 1) to 1 (full sensitivity, K<sub>f</sub> = K<sub>t</sub>), so K<sub>f</sub> always lies between 1 and K<sub>t</sub>.

Data books give q against notch radius r for each class of steel. Neuber's estimate q = 1/(1 + √a/√r) shows the trend: √a is a material constant in √mm and r is the notch radius in mm. A larger r raises q, and a stronger steel has a smaller √a, which also raises q. For a 600 MPa steel in bending √a ≈ 0.38 √mm, so q = 0.72 at r = 1 mm and 0.84 at r = 4 mm. Grey cast iron is the exception: its graphite flakes already act as internal notches, so an external notch adds little and q is low (about 0.2).

Under a steady load a ductile part yields locally at the notch, the peak spreads out, and design on the nominal stress is usually enough. A brittle material cannot yield, so its static check uses K<sub>t</sub> σ<sub>nom</sub>. Every fatigue check uses K<sub>f</sub>, for ductile and brittle materials alike.

A gentler stress path lowers K<sub>t</sub>: a larger fillet radius, a taper instead of a step, a sled-runner keyway instead of an end-milled one, or small extra holes beside a loaded hole so the stress lines bend gradually. A larger r lowers K<sub>t</sub> and raises q; the fall in K<sub>t</sub> usually wins, so K<sub>f</sub> falls.

When a shoulder must stay square for a bearing, a relief groove (a shallow undercut) gives room for a bigger radius. Thread roots and keyway corners, with their tiny radii, are the usual crack starters.

items: Use K<sub>f</sub> in fatigue and K<sub>t</sub> for a brittle part under static load.
Take σ<sub>nom</sub> on the net section, as the chart does.
Pick the chart for the load: axial, bending and torsion curves differ.
Apply the notch factor once: if a data book already divides S<sub>e</sub> by K<sub>f</sub>, do not multiply the stress by K<sub>f</sub> too.

figure.caption: The three lines show how Kf rises from 1 toward Kt as q goes from 0 to 1. The diagonal is full sensitivity; a real material lies on a line set by its q.

spec.aria: Three straight lines of fatigue notch factor against theoretical stress concentration factor for notch sensitivity zero, one half and one; the q = 1 line is the full diagonal.

examples.question: A stepped shaft has d = 40 mm, D = 50 mm and a fillet of radius r = 4 mm. It carries a fully reversed bending moment of amplitude M = 300 N·m. For D/d = 1.25 and r/d = 0.10 the bending chart gives K<sub>t</sub> = 1.6, and the steel has √a = 0.38 √mm. Find the nominal stress, the elastic peak stress, q, K<sub>f</sub> and the fatigue-effective stress at the fillet.
steps: Elastic peak: σ<sub>max</sub> = K<sub>t</sub> σ<sub>nom</sub> = 1.6 × 47.75 = 76.39 MPa.
examples.answer: σ<sub>nom</sub> = 47.75 MPa, σ<sub>max</sub> = 76.39 MPa, q = 0.84, K<sub>f</sub> = 1.50 and the fatigue check uses 71.8 MPa. For comparison, the larger section carries only 32 × 300 000/(π × 50³) = 24.4 MPa.

examples.question: A steel plate 60 mm wide and 10 mm thick has a central hole of 12 mm diameter. It carries an axial load that alternates between +36 kN and −36 kN, and the steel has q = 0.9 at this hole. Find the nominal stress, K<sub>t</sub> by Heywood's formula, the peak stress and the fatigue-effective stress.
steps: σ<sub>nom</sub> = 36 000/480 = 75.0 MPa (the gross section would give 36 000/600 = 60 MPa, which is not what the formula uses).
examples.answer: σ<sub>nom</sub> = 75 MPa, K<sub>t</sub> = 2.51, peak 188.4 MPa, K<sub>f</sub> = 2.36 and a fatigue-effective amplitude of 177.1 MPa: the small hole more than doubles the stress the plate's fatigue check must carry.

traps: Using K<sub>t</sub> in a fatigue calculation. Fatigue uses K<sub>f</sub> = 1 + q(K<sub>t</sub> − 1), which is smaller unless q = 1.
Taking σ<sub>nom</sub> on the gross area: in the plate example 60 MPa instead of 75 MPa, a peak 20 % too low.
Reading the bending chart for a torsion load. The curves differ for axial, bending and torsion.
Calling K<sub>t</sub> a material property. K<sub>t</sub> depends only on geometry and load type; q (and so K<sub>f</sub>) depends on the material and the radius.
Applying the notch twice: multiplying the stress by K<sub>f</sub> after the data book has already divided S<sub>e</sub> by K<sub>f</sub>.

quiz.q: Define K<sub>t</sub> and q, and write K<sub>f</sub> in terms of them.
quiz.a: K<sub>t</sub> = σ<sub>max</sub>/σ<sub>nom</sub> on the net section; q = (K<sub>f</sub> − 1)/(K<sub>t</sub> − 1); K<sub>f</sub> = 1 + q(K<sub>t</sub> − 1).

quiz.q: Why is K<sub>f</sub> never greater than K<sub>t</sub>?
quiz.a: q lies between 0 and 1, so K<sub>f</sub> = 1 + q(K<sub>t</sub> − 1) runs from 1 to K<sub>t</sub>; the material can feel at most the full elastic concentration.

quiz.q: A part has σ<sub>nom</sub> = 60 MPa, K<sub>t</sub> = 1.9 and q = 0.8. Find K<sub>f</sub> and the fatigue-effective stress.
A ductile steel shaft with K<sub>t</sub> = 2.5 carries a steady load only. Should K<sub>t</sub> be used in its static design? Explain.
quiz.a: Usually not: the peak yields locally and spreads, so design on the nominal stress. K<sub>t</sub> is for brittle materials, K<sub>f</sub> for repeated loads.

quiz.q: With √a = 0.38 √mm, find q for fillet radii of 1 mm and 4 mm.
In q = 1/(1 + √a/√r), a larger r raises q. Why does a larger fillet still usually lower K<sub>f</sub>?
quiz.a: A larger r also lowers K<sub>t</sub>, and K<sub>f</sub> = 1 + q(K<sub>t</sub> − 1). The fall in (K<sub>t</sub> − 1) is usually larger than the rise in q, so their product, and so K<sub>f</sub>, falls.

beyond: Not for the exam. Finite element software now computes Kt for complex CAD shapes where no chart exists, and fatigue standards use notch rules to turn elastic peaks into fatigue-effective stresses. Additive manufacturing adds surface roughness and internal pores that act as many tiny notches. Search for 'Peterson stress concentration factors', 'Neuber notch sensitivity' and 'stress flow lines' to go deeper.
